subject: mrcp-statistics
title: Sensitivity, specificity and screening

steps.tx: **Sensitivity** is the proportion of people with the disease who test positive. **Specificity** is the proportion without the disease who test negative. Both are properties of the test itself and do not change with how common the disease is. A highly sensitive test has few false negatives, so a negative result helps rule disease out, summarised by SnNout. A highly specific test has few false positives, so a positive result helps rule disease in, summarised by SpPIn.
steps.say: Sensitivity is the proportion of people with the disease who test positive. Specificity is the proportion without the disease who test negative. Both belong to the test itself and do not change with how common the disease is. A highly sensitive test has few false negatives, so a negative result helps rule disease out, summarised by SnNout. A highly specific test has few false positives, so a positive result helps rule disease in, summarised by SpPIn.

steps.tx: **Positive predictive value** depends on **prevalence** as well as on **sensitivity** and **specificity**. When a condition is uncommon, the large healthy group generates many **false positives**, and these can outnumber the **true positives** even when the test performs well. Sketching a hypothetical cohort in a two by two grid makes this pattern easy to see and check for yourself.
steps.say: Positive predictive value depends on prevalence as well as on sensitivity and specificity. When a condition is uncommon, the large healthy group generates many false positives, and these can outnumber the true positives even when the test performs well. Sketching a hypothetical cohort in a two by two grid makes this pattern easy to see and check for yourself.

steps.tx: A **likelihood ratio** shows how much a result changes the odds of disease, and it does not depend on prevalence. The positive likelihood ratio equals sensitivity divided by one minus specificity. Post-test odds equal pre-test odds multiplied by the likelihood ratio. Convert the pre-test probability to odds, multiply, then convert back to a probability. A positive likelihood ratio of 4 applied to a pre-test probability of 50% gives a post-test probability of 80%.

The positive likelihood ratio equals sensitivity divided by one minus specificity. Post-test odds equal pre-test odds multiplied by the likelihood ratio. Convert the pre-test probability to odds, multiply, then convert back to a probability. A positive likelihood ratio of four applied to a pre-test probability of fifty percent gives a post-test probability of eighty percent.

steps.tx: **Serial** testing, where all tests must be positive, raises **specificity** but lowers **sensitivity**. **Parallel** testing, where any positive counts, does the reverse. Under conditional independence, joint sensitivity for a serial pair is the product of the individual sensitivities. Two tests with sensitivity and specificity of 90% each give serial sensitivity of 81% and serial specificity of about 99%. The choice depends on whether missed cases or unnecessary investigation is the greater harm.
steps.say: Serial testing, where all tests must be positive, raises specificity but lowers sensitivity. Parallel testing, where any positive counts, does the reverse. Under conditional independence, joint sensitivity for a serial pair is the product of the individual sensitivities. Two tests each with ninety percent sensitivity and specificity give serial sensitivity of eighty-one percent and serial specificity of about ninety-nine percent. The choice depends on whether missed cases or unnecessary investigation is the greater harm.

steps.tx: Screening should be judged on **mortality**, not on survival from diagnosis. **Lead-time bias** occurs when early detection lengthens survival measured from diagnosis without changing the date of death, so survival looks better. **Overdiagnosis** detects disease that would never have caused harm, inflating incidence without reducing deaths. Absolute measures matter too: moving cancer mortality from 4 in 100 to 3 in 100 is a 25% relative reduction but a number needed to screen of 100.
